sections.h2: Orleans Parish and the City of New Orleans
sections.html: The parish line and the New Orleans city limit are the same line, a match that dates to 1870. The 2020 census counted 383,997 people here, and the 2025 estimate is 362,184. One local government runs zoning, code enforcement and tax billing, so a seller's paperwork mostly stays in one building.

Your bill involves three bodies. The Assessor decides value and signs off on exemptions. The Bureau of the Treasury, a city department, sends bills and takes payment. The City Council acts as the Board of Review when someone contests a value.

A bill that keeps coming after you sold should go to the Assessor, which updates ownership and mailing addresses. Treasury also answers common billing questions on its FAQ page.

sections.h2: Due dates, interest and how to pay
sections.html:
The usual due date is January 31, with 1 percent interest added each month to what is unpaid. Bills typically mail in late December, but timing moves with the city's millage vote and the print schedule. Some years the city pushes the deadline later. Most Louisiana parishes use December 31 instead. Selling in early winter? Trust the date printed on your bill.

A bill that never showed up still earns interest, penalty and costs. Search the tax payment portal for yours, or call (504) 658-1712.

  • Online e-checks cost nothing extra.
  • A third-party fee of about 2.49 percent applies to cards.
  • Regular payments can be cash, check or money order.
  • Partial payments work in person or by mail only. They do not halt interest or tax sale costs.

The Assessor estimates fair market value, and only a slice of it is taxed. A home's land and its residential improvements are each assessed at 10 percent of market value, while commercial improvements are assessed at 15 percent. Millage is then applied to what remains after any exemption.

sections.h2: Homestead exemption and the age freeze
sections.html:
If you own and occupy the house, the homestead exemption removes the first $75,000 of market value (that is, $7,500 of assessed value) from the taxable base.

Orleans is unusual here. The exemption reduces municipal property taxes, which it does not do elsewhere in Louisiana.

  • The exemption is tied to you as the occupant. Whoever buys and moves in files a new application.
  • Without a homestead exemption on your bill, payments first satisfy recorded municipal liens, such as code enforcement liens, and only then your taxes (City Code 6-39(d)). An occupied homestead is spared, except when it holds a short-term rental permit or the lien comes from a Chapter 26 violation.

Owners aged 65 or older with qualifying income may apply for the special assessment freeze. It stops on December 31 of the year of a sale or the owner's death, so it never passes to a buyer.

Raise it with the Assessor while the rolls are open for public inspection. If you still disagree, file a written appeal with the Board of Review. The City Council posts a calendar each year. In the recent cycle, public inspection began in mid-July and the filing deadline fell in the third week of August. Hearings run in September at Delgado Community College, City Park Campus, and written decisions follow in October. Check the Council appeals page for the current dates.

The Board accepts three kinds of evidence:

  • The recent sale price of your property.
  • Recent sale prices of comparable properties nearby.
  • The opinion of a real estate professional.

Appraisals, insurance policies, photographs and contractor repair estimates all help support a claim of damage or over-valuation. Send the form and every supporting paper together, since an incomplete appeal is denied. A Board decision you dislike can go to the Louisiana Tax Commission, by written appeal within 10 business days of the notice. The Board cannot rule on homestead denials or age freeze decisions.

Act 718 of 2018 lets homeowners spread a big tax increase over four years when an assessment rose by more than 50 percent in a reassessment year. Qualifying parcels carry an "Act 718" marker on the tax bill.

Orleans was reassessed in two phases: 75 percent of the city for the 2020 tax year and the remaining 25 percent for 2021. Owners without a homestead exemption in the year of implementation do not qualify, and neither do commercial owners.

Someone who buys a property already under Act 718 does not get the phase-in, which means the first bill for the new owner may exceed yours. If an appeal lowers the assessment below the 50 percent threshold, the phase-in ends and a revised bill for the full amount comes due.

New tax sale and adjudication rules started on January 1, 2026. Under the earlier system, an owner could redeem for roughly three years after the tax sale certificate was recorded. A valid blight judgment shortens that to 18 months, and adjudications can run three to five years. Call the Treasury for how the current process affects your parcel.

To redeem an older sale, you pay:

  • The amount the tax sale purchaser paid at the sale.
  • Interest of 1 percent per month until redeemed.
  • A 5 percent penalty.
  • The current year's taxes and other debts.

Tax sale costs can also appear as a line on a bill, covering the work of preparing a property for the upcoming sale. A tax sale claim or code lien shows up in a title search, and whoever closes the sale has to account for it.

The title company or attorney uncovers unpaid taxes and liens and settles them from your proceeds at closing. Ahead of that day, confirm your bill status, any municipal liens and whether your homestead exemption is on file.

Under R.S. 47:1993, Louisiana attaches a lien to each assessed property when the assessment roll is delivered to the recorder of mortgages. That lien generally ranks ahead of other encumbrances, apart from prior-year rolls and tax lien certificates, so unpaid taxes must be settled before clean title passes.

Land Records, at 1340 Poydras Street, takes deeds weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Certified copies run $30 each plus copy charges. Margins matter: 2 inches at the top of the first sheet and 1 inch elsewhere, or the clerk may reject the document or add a $20 surcharge.

faqs.q: What is the property tax due date in Orleans Parish?
faqs.a: Bills are usually due January 31, and interest runs at 1 percent per month after the due date. The city does not waive it for a bill that was never received.

faqs.q: Who do I call if I sold my house but still get the bill?
faqs.a: Call the Orleans Parish Assessor at (504) 754-8811. That office handles ownership and mailing address changes and can update the account.

faqs.q: What is the Orleans Parish homestead exemption?
faqs.a: It is $7,500 of assessed value, which equals $75,000 of market value, on a home you own and live in. In Orleans it applies to municipal taxes as well, unlike most of Louisiana.

faqs.q: Can I pay Orleans Parish property tax online?
faqs.a: Yes. Online e-check payments have no service fee, and card payments carry a fee of about 2.49 percent. Partial payments cannot be made online, so those must be mailed or paid in person at City Hall.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal to the Louisiana Tax Commission?
faqs.a: You have 10 business days after the Board of Review's notice is postmarked or delivered. The appeal must be in writing, and forms are linked from the City Council's appeals page.
